ads.primary_text:
You run a business, and somewhere in your admin there's an online store that's built and just sitting there. Maybe three or four of them.

You open the dashboard to check on something else, and there they are. Logo done. Pages done. Ready to be loaded. Nobody has touched them in months, maybe years, because the business in front of you needed you first. The marketing slowed down, the week filled up, and the stores waited.

Here's the part nobody says out loud. A built store is not a running store. What decides a store comes after it goes live: choosing the first products, testing them, reading the results, replacing what doesn't sell. The build ended when the store was ready, so nobody was ever assigned to that part. Your stores didn't fail. Nobody was on them.

So Readymerce built the $500 Build around the part after launch. In order:

Before launch: a fit call to agree the platform (Shopify or Etsy) and scope with you. Research on demand and competition picks your niche and first products from data, not a hunch. Then a new store, opened in your name, with the logo, banner, structure, listings and shipping profiles done.

At launch: products go live in stages instead of one big drop. They get small, controlled ad tests on a budget you approve.

After launch: an early performance review, in a report you can read, on what to keep, replace or roll out next. Then the corrections: ads monitored and adjusted, listings worked on.

You approve the budgets and read the reports. We do the testing, the adjustments and the listing work.

The store account is in your name and stays in your name. Payouts go to your bank account. The brand, listings and images belong to you.

The $500 is one-time and doesn't cover ad spend, product costs or platform fees. Ongoing work after launch is agreed on that fit call, and any fee for it is quoted there. There's a 7-day refund on the $500 fee, counted from the day you pay. It ends early if you approve the delivered store, buy any add-on or upgrade, or ask for more work. And we don't promise sales or income. Nobody honest can.

Every month those stores sit is another month with nothing tested.

Not just sitting.

ads.headline: marketing's slowed down so much and my stores are just sitting there

ads.name: C1-V3
ads.primary_text:
I've never said this out loud, not even to my accountant. I have three online stores built and sitting in the admin, and I haven't done anything with them in years.

I run a small clothing shop. The back room is where I do the books, at a desk wedged between two rails of stock and a box of spare hangers.

Every March my accountant sits in that room with me and goes through the year line by line. This year he stopped on the platform fees.

"What are these three?" he asked.

"My online stores," I said.

"How are they doing?"

"Slow," I said. Which was a lie. Slow would have meant something was happening.

The truth is they were built. Themes picked, pages set up, a few products half chosen. Ready to be loaded, and just sitting there. I had been paying every month for three stores nobody had visited in years.

He didn't push. He made a small pencil mark next to the line and moved on. I remember that mark more than anything else he said that day.

After he left I sat there with the laptop shut. It was 6:40. The shop was closed. I could hear the rail creak when the heating came on. I didn't open it.

I didn't know yet that the thing that changed it would be a stranger with a pen at the shipping counter.

Anyway. I should back up.

I bought this shop with most of what I had saved. It was supposed to be the steady part. The online side was supposed to be the growth.

For a few years the marketing was the one bringing in the money. Then it slowed down so much that some weeks the door barely opened.

The first store I built myself, over a winter of evenings. It went live in November. By the second week of December I was packing orders at midnight, sending them off late, and apologizing to people I had never met. I'm good at a lot of things, but I have very little time.

"I had one before," I would tell people later. "I just ended it because I was dealing with a lot."

The second store I built in a weekend, full of good intentions. It never had a single product loaded.

For the third, I did what everyone says to do. I asked about hiring someone.

I got three quotes. $5,000. $20,000. $15,000.

I'm like, seriously? Come on.

I would not pay $2,500 to anybody unless I could see some results. Let alone twenty thousand.

What I actually wanted was someone to fully automate my online business. I would have paid for that. Just not twenty thousand dollars of it, up front, on a promise.

So I built the third one myself too. Watched the videos, picked a theme, and it went live on a Sunday afternoon. Then Monday came, the shop needed me, and it sat.

I added it up once. Three stores. The monthly fees. A theme I paid for twice. The weekends I will never get back. I stopped adding.

Some nights I would open the admin, look at the three store names, and close it again without clicking anything. It felt like opening a drawer of bills.

What I told myself was always the same. I'm not a computer person. I don't have the time. I can't compete with the big stores anyway.

None of that turned out to be the reason.

The reason showed up on an ordinary Sunday, doing stock in the shop.

I was moving the scarves to the front because they had sold. I was marking down a jacket that hadn't moved in six weeks. I was changing the window. And somewhere between the price gun and the mannequin, I realized I had done this every single week for eleven years.

That's the job. Opening day isn't the job. The job is every week after it. See what sells, move it forward, take out what doesn't, bring in the next thing.

I would never open up once, flip the sign, and walk away for three years.

That is exactly what happened to all three of my stores.

That night I went looking for why. I found the platform's own guide for people who build stores for clients. It says the builder can "transfer ownership to the client when it's ready to go live."

Ready to go live. That is where the builder's job is designed to end.

Here is what I finally understood. On launch day a store is a set of guesses. Which products. Which photos. Which price. Which words in the title. The first weeks after it opens are when those guesses finally get tested by real people. Somebody clicks and leaves. One product gets looked at and nothing else does. A listing gets no attention at all.

That information is worth nothing unless somebody reads it and acts on it. Fix the listing. Drop the product nobody wants. Put the next one live. Test it small. Read it again.

Nobody was assigned to that work on my stores. Not the builder, whose job ended on launch day. Not me, because the shop takes the whole day. So each store froze on the day it went live and stayed exactly like that.

It wasn't the platform, and it wasn't me. A built store is not a running store, and nobody had the job of running mine.

Which raised a worse question. Who would take that job? I didn't have the hours, and the people who did wanted twenty thousand dollars.

I got my answer in a queue.

A few days later I was at the shipping counter with two returns. The woman ahead of me had a stack of small parcels, all labeled. Online orders.

I said something like, "I've got online stores too."

She turned around. "So who's working on them?"

I opened my mouth to answer and realized nobody ever had.

Her first store, she said, had been handed over the day it went live, and the builder disappeared. Then she took the pen from the counter, turned my receipt over, and drew two lines. A short one and a long one.

"Everyone quotes you this," she said, tapping the short one. Then the long one. "This is the part that decides it."

A small team built the store she has now, in her name, and they're still on it. Products go live in stages, small ad tests on a budget she approves, and a written review of what to keep and what to replace.

"It's not automatic," she said. "I approve the budget and read what they send. I just don't do the work."

She wrote a name under the two lines. Readymerce. Then she was gone.

I didn't trust it. I pay $500 and then I'm going to have to pay more money down the road, I thought.

So I read their page the way my accountant reads a receipt.

The $500 is one-time. The store is opened in your name and stays in your name. Products are picked from search demand and competition data and go live in stages, each with a small ad test on a budget you approve. After launch: an early performance review, corrections, new products.

Then the part most companies bury. Product costs, platform fees and ad spend are yours, not in the $500. The ongoing work is quoted on the call before you commit. No income guarantees. I trusted that more than a promise.

The refund I read twice. Seven days from payment, the $500 fee only, and it ends when you accept delivery, buy any add-on, or ask for more work.

On the call I said it straight. Show me exactly what the $500 pays for. They did, line by line, including after launch day. And they said it isn't fully automatic. I approve budgets and read reports. They do the work.

My own stores sat because the shop needed me. The agencies wanted $5,000 to $20,000 before I saw anything. A builder hands it over on launch day. This was $500, every other cost named, and the work after launch on the list.

"I'll start with the 500," I said.

It was a new store, built in my name, on the platform we agreed on the call. The first time I logged in, my own name was in the owner field. I looked at it longer than I'd like to admit.

Products went live in stages, the first test on a budget I approved. What to do next was no longer my job.

Then the first written review came in.

I opened it in the back room at 6:40, shop closed, the rail creaking. The laptop was open this time.

It said what to keep. What to replace, and why. Which listings they had already fixed, and what was going live next.

It was the first time in years anyone had done anything with a store of mine after launch day.

Relief, mostly. Like someone had finally walked into a room I had left the lights on in for three years.

The next March, my accountant stopped on the platform fees again. I told him the truth. Three stores that sat. One that's live, in my name, with a team still on it. He rubbed out his pencil mark.

If I could tell the owner I was that night at 6:40 one thing, it would be this. You didn't fail at building stores. You built three. Nobody ever had the job of working them after they went live.

Every month mine sat, I paid for stores that did nothing. The $500 Build is what I started with, in my name, in stages, on a budget I approve. And they stay after launch day.

The receipt with the two lines is still on my desk.

P.S. The build was never the hard part. Ask anyone you talk to the question she asked me: who's working on it after it goes live? Mine finally has someone. It's loaded and live.

The marketing was the thing bringing in the money. The week it slowed down was the week I finally looked at the online stores I'd forgotten I owned.
A woman at the shipping counter asked me one question about my online stores. "So who's working on them?" I had no answer.

ads.headline: Ive had 2 stores on Shopify both failed

ads.name: C2-V3
ads.primary_text:
$254 for my first store. About $750 for the second. It took one number I had never bothered to count to explain both of them.

Store one ended at our kitchen table on a Sunday night. My wife was asleep, the laptop was open, and the dashboard said about 600 clicks in three weeks and zero orders. I kept hitting refresh like the zero was a glitch.

Forty-four dollars for the website. Two hundred and ten on ads. I added it up on the back of an envelope, $254, and wrote a zero next to it for the sales.

The next morning I told her the store had been "a test." I didn't mention I'd already picked a name for the second one.

That envelope is still in our kitchen drawer. There are two more numbers on it now, one in blue pen and one in pencil, and the smallest one is the one that changed everything.

Why a store at all? I sell solar on commission. Some months are great. Some months the homeowners just aren't interested, and you feel it at the grocery store. I wanted something steadier that was mine. Just something that didn't depend on a stranger in a driveway saying yes.

Anyway. Let me back up.

Store one sold posture correctors. I found the product the way a lot of people do, from a video of a guy saying it was about to blow up. I built the store over two weekends, turned on a $50 ad set, and waited.

Clicks came in. Sales didn't.

So I did what the forums said. I posted my numbers, still no sales, about 600 clicks, and people answered fast. Your landing page. Your targeting. You need more traffic.

I tried new interests. Same product, more clicks, still no sales.

I installed everything. Reviews, discounts, an email pop-up, trust badges, a cleaner product page. No one had bought anything.

I paid for one of those one-week store challenges. I failed the challenge too.

After three weeks I stopped. The product did not sell, so I had to close the store. That's how I explained it to myself, and that's how I explained it to my brother.

Eleven months later I opened store two anyway and told myself I'd learned my lesson.

Store two sold chess boards. Nicer theme, better photos. After ten days of ads, still no orders. People came. Nobody bought. Nobody even put one in a cart.

At 1am one night I typed "I am growing tired of looking at all the traffic and no sales" into a forum, then deleted it. Nobody was going to tell me anything new.

When you do all that work just to find out people don't even want the thing you're selling, it's extremely discouraging. It makes you want to give up. So I did, faster than the first time. I had to stop or I was going to lose all my money.

It felt like pure loss. Money, time, energy, and honestly hope.

For months after that, if anyone brought up online stores, I'd say "I tried dropshipping" the way people say "I tried running." The videos make it seem like easy money when it's really not, and I had decided I wasn't one of the people it works for. I definitely was not an expert.

Then my wife cleaned out the kitchen drawer, held up the envelope, and asked, "What's this?"

Under the $254, in blue pen, was store two: theme, apps, plan fees, ads. About $750. A little over a thousand dollars total.

Then I counted something I had never counted. How many products had those two stores actually tested? I wrote the answer under the money in pencil.

2.

One product per store. A thousand dollars and the better part of two years, and my stores had tested two products.

I looked up what a normal store converts at. A Shopify analytics company publishes the average, and it's about 1.4 percent. Of every hundred visits, a little over one turns into an order. So I ran my own numbers. About 600 clicks at an average store's rate is around eight orders. That's an average, not a promise. But it isn't zero.

Zero isn't what you get when a store is a little off. Zero is what you get when the people come, look at the one thing on the shelf, and don't want it. My traffic was fine. My trust badges were fine. The product missed, and the store never got a second one.

That's why nothing I tried moved. New interests brought more people to the same product. Reviews and badges polished the shelf around the same product. The challenge put a deadline on the same single guess. Every fix was aimed at the store. Not one of them changed what was on the shelf.

A product-research guide I found that week said it plainly: "Most successful dropshippers test 5 to 10 products before finding one that scales profitably."

Five to ten. I had tested two, in two separate stores, and called myself a failure both times.

I didn't have two failed stores. I had two stores that each got one shot, and one guess misses a lot more often than it hits.

That felt lighter and worse. Lighter because it wasn't me. Worse because I still couldn't do anything with it. I couldn't afford five to ten more rounds of what I'd been doing, one product at a time with ads running until the money ran out. That way had cost me a thousand dollars for two answers.

So the envelope went back in the drawer.

A few weeks later, in a tire shop waiting room, I was doing commission math on the back of that same envelope because it was the only paper in my truck.

The woman in the next chair glanced over. "Two fifty-four and a zero. Rough ratio."

I laughed and told her the whole thing in ninety seconds. She'd bought stock for a small chain of gift shops most of her working life, and she asked one question.

"How many products did you put on the shelf?"

"One," I said. "Per store."

"We never stock one thing and wait," she said. "We put a few new things out in small amounts, watch what moves, and send back what doesn't. Most of it doesn't. You don't close the shop because one item sat. You pull the item."

Then the line I still repeat: "You didn't run two stores. You ran one product twice."

That night I searched for what she described and found a page that said it almost word for word. A company called Readymerce builds the store in your name, then releases products in stages instead of one single drop, each with controlled ad testing on a budget you approve. An early performance review decides what stays. What doesn't sell gets replaced with new products, picked from search demand and competition data.

My first reaction wasn't "finally." It was "here we go." I've been burned many times, and a lot of these companies fake the reviews, so I skipped the testimonials and read the fine print.

What got me was a section called "What Is NOT Included": product costs, platform fees, ad spend, and any income, sales or profitability guarantee. Every guru I'd paid made it seem like easy money. This was the first page that agreed with me that it isn't.

On the call I asked straight out: is it $500 and then it goes up to $5,000? It's $500 for the build, one time. The ad budget for the tests is mine, and I set it. Anything past the build, like how much ongoing help, gets quoted on that call.

The refund is seven days from payment, on the $500 fee only, and it ends when you accept delivery, buy any add-on, or ask for further work. Narrow, but written plainly. And the store and its payouts would be in my name either way.

When it was ready, I logged in and checked the owner field first. My name.

The first products went live in stages, each with a test budget I'd approved before a dollar was spent. I knew the most any test could cost me before it started.

The first product didn't do much. Old me would have closed the store that night. Instead the early review came in writing: which product to keep testing, which to replace, and why, with the replacement already lined up. Someone was still on my store after it went live, reading the numbers I used to stare at alone at midnight.

My wife read it over my shoulder. She's watched me close two stores. "So they're not giving up on it."

No. And neither am I.

The store is still open, in my name. The first stage is tested, the first written review is in my hands, and the team is still on it after launch day. For the first time in three tries, a product that didn't sell didn't mean the store was dead. Sunday nights I don't sit there hitting refresh anymore. And when someone brings up online stores, I don't say "I tried." I say I have one.

It was never really the dollars. It was the number of shots. What I needed was a store in my name that gets more than one: products in stages, each with a small test on a budget I approve, and someone who reviews the results and replaces what doesn't sell.

It starts with the $500 Build. Ad spend, product costs and platform fees are extra, and they say so before you pay. No income promise, and I wouldn't trust one.

I was afraid to ever try again. Eventually I did. If I'd stopped at store two, one product nobody wanted would have been the last word on me. Give the next one what mine never got. A second shot.

P.S. The smallest number on that envelope is in pencil. 2. If I'd counted after store one, I'd have skipped store two.

Two stores, both closed, and I only ever told my family about the first one.
11:48pm on a Sunday, I posted my store's numbers in a forum and asked a room full of strangers what I was doing wrong.
My second store didn't close for the reason I told everyone. It took a woman in a tire shop waiting room to tell me the real one.
The night I closed my second store I felt relieved, and I hated myself for feeling relieved.

The store account is in your name and stays in your name. Payouts go to your bank account. The brand, listings and images belong to you.

The $500 is one-time and doesn't cover ad spend, product costs or platform fees. Ongoing work after launch is agreed on that fit call, and any fee for it is quoted there. There's a 7-day refund on the $500 fee, counted from the day you pay. It ends early if you approve the delivered store, buy any add-on or upgrade, or ask for more work. And we don't promise sales or income. Nobody honest can.

Every month those stores sit is another month with nothing tested.

Not just sitting.

ads.primary_text:
"Nobody quits to start one," the guy from purchasing said in the break room. He wasn't even talking to me.

I've worked receiving at a distribution center for eleven years. All day I scan other people's products. Phone stands, dog beds, candle kits, boxes of stuff somebody is selling online. I check them in and send them on.

For five of those years I had my own store idea sitting in a folder on my laptop, with a closed store behind it that almost nobody knew about.

My wife knew. Nobody at work did.

What nobody knew about was the car. Most mornings I'd park, turn the engine off and just sit there with my hands on the wheel. Some days I'd say it out loud. "Come on, man. I wish I was doing something else." Then I'd clip my badge on and go in.

Same spot, same thermos, same sentence.

I was forty-one. I figured I'd be saying it in that parking spot at fifty-one.

It took one sentence in a break room, and it wasn't even meant for me, to show me what I'd had backwards the whole time.

Let me back up.

I earn good money. Not rich. Good, with benefits I actually need. And every plan I ever made for the store hit the same wall: I don't want to quit and then start struggling.

So I did what you do. I did it after hours.

The first two years went to figuring out which platform was even the right one. Every answer opened three more tabs.

Then I built one. One product, picked the way you pick a lottery number, on a gut feeling on a Sunday. The listings, photos and shipping settings ate my evenings for two months. Much more complicated to set up and manage than any video made it look.

I ran ads on weekends and checked them on my breaks. It didn't sell one product. Not one.

Then overtime season hit. Twelve-hour days. I'd get home after nine, open the laptop and wake up an hour later with my boots on and the dashboard still glowing. In January I closed the store, because I didn't have time to try and work the business to see sales.

My wife never said I told you so. She just stopped asking about it, which was worse.

After that I got careful. I watched the walk-out-on-your-job ads and the course ads, and bought neither. I'm not lazy. I just don't wanna be trained to do it. I already have a job.

So I made a rule. When I'm ready, I'll do it properly: save up, give notice, go full time. "I got till October." October came and went. So did the next one.

Once, in the car after a shift, I did the math on the back of a pay stub. Five years, two evenings a week. Over five hundred evenings I'd given that idea, and my store got maybe one real try out of all of them.

I figured that said something about me.

Then, a few weeks ago, a kid from the night crew told the break room he was quitting in the spring because his online store was about to take off. The guy from purchasing didn't look up from his sandwich.

"Nobody quits to start one," he said. Flat, the way he says everything. Then he went back to eating.

He wasn't talking to me. I was two tables over, and my ears went hot like he'd said it straight to me.

Because quitting to start one was my plan.

And here's the part that should have been obvious, to me of all people.

At work, a new item never shows up as a truckload. Purchasing orders a small trial first. If it moves, they reorder. If it doesn't, it's gone next month and nobody takes it personally. I've checked in thousands of those trial orders. Nobody ever bets the building on one.

My store was one truckload of one guess.

And my plan was to make that bet bigger. Wait until I was ready, quit, and put my paycheck behind the next guess.

That afternoon in the car I finally looked up how stores that actually sell find the thing that sells. One practitioner guide put it plainly: "Most successful dropshippers test 5 to 10 products before finding one that scales profitably."

A new store's first weeks aren't a build. They're a loop. Pick a product, put a small ad budget behind it, read what happened, cut what isn't moving, put the next one up. Again and again, like trial orders on my dock. It runs on weekdays, not Sunday nights.

Somebody with a full-time job can do the build once. After that he gets one pass through the loop, maybe, in leftover hours. When that one guess misses, it looks like the idea failed. It didn't. One guess only proved one guess missed.

That's the one-shot launch, and that's what killed my store. Not my job, and not me.

It's also why waiting never helped. Waiting until you're ready doesn't add a single test. It just makes the eventual bet bigger. And quitting first doesn't fix the one shot. It puts your salary on it.

So the job was never the risky part. It was the safe part. What I needed was the loop running in somebody's working day, at a cost I set, while my paycheck kept coming.

I didn't know anybody who did that.

Two days later the purchasing guy sat across from me, because mine was the only open seat. I asked what he'd meant.

He shrugged. His wife had wanted a store for years but wouldn't touch it while she was working. She'd been reading about a place that builds the store in your name and puts products up in stages, a small test on each, on a budget you approve, while you keep your job. She hadn't signed up. He just liked the logic. "It's how I'd buy," he said. "Small first."

Before his break ended he texted me the name. Readymerce.

I didn't trust it. I've seen a hundred of these. So I asked for the full contract before making payment, printed the terms and the refund policy, and read them on my breaks with a pen.

In writing: $500 one-time for the build. The store in my name, staying in my name, payouts to my bank. Product costs, platform fees and ad spend extra and mine, with every test budget one I approve. Not a course. And on page after page, no income promises.

That last line is what got me. Every pitch I'd ever heard gave me a number. This one refused to.

I circled the refund. Seven days from payment, the $500 build fee only, and it ends the moment you accept the delivery, buy any add-on or upgrade, or ask for further work. Platform fees and ad spend never come back. In the margin I wrote: if the build isn't done inside a week, what is that protecting? Not much, and they don't pretend otherwise.

So my safety was the list, not the refund. Every cost named before I spent a dollar, the store in my name, a test budget I'd type myself. And the paycheck still landing every Friday.

On the call they settled what I'd been stuck on for two years, Shopify or Etsy, and agreed how much the team keeps doing after launch. I paid on my lunch break, sitting in the car. Got the confirmation email and went back to the dock.

The store opened in my name. I checked the owner field on my break like a man checking a lottery ticket.

The products were picked from search demand and competition data, not a gut feeling on a Sunday, and they went live in stages. The first stage got a small test, on a budget I approved from my phone between two trucks.

I didn't open the laptop at night. Not once. I ate dinner at the table with my wife.

Then the first review came, written. I read it in the parked car after my shift. Which products to keep, which to replace, what goes in the next stage. Somebody had run the loop on my store in their working day.

I was sitting in the exact spot where I used to say I wish I was doing something else. And I was doing something else. It was just happening while I was at work.

The team is still on it. The next stage, the corrections, the reports I can check whenever I want. My store doesn't get my leftover hours anymore. It gets somebody's real ones.

I still clock in at six. I still earn good money. I didn't quit anything. For the first time in five years the store exists, in my name, being worked on, and my salary never had to be the bet.

Last week the purchasing guy asked how the thing was going. I showed him the review on my phone. He read it the way he reads a trial order, nodded and said, "Small first."

If you're reading this in a parked car before a shift, here's what I wish somebody had told me. The job isn't what's stopping you. It's the safe part. What stopped me was the one-shot launch: one guessed product, all at once, in the hours after work.

Several small tests, on a budget you approve, run in somebody's working day while the paycheck keeps coming, is a different bet. You don't get trained. And the store is in your name.

That's the $500 Build. You see what's included and what isn't on the call, and you can read every term before you pay. I did. Twice.

P.S. Waiting until I was ready cost me five years and over five hundred evenings, and my store got one shot out of all of them. Yours should get more than one.

The $500 Build: your store built and opened in your name, products released in stages, each tested on a budget you approve, a written review of what to keep and what to replace, and a team still working on it after launch. Ad spend, product costs and platform fees are extra. The refund window is 7 days from payment, covers the $500 build fee only, and ends when you accept delivery, buy any add-on or upgrade, or ask for further work. No income promises.

Start without quitting.

9:47pm, kitchen table, boots still on. I'd fallen asleep in front of my own store's ad dashboard again, and it still said zero orders.
For five years I told my wife I'd start the store when I was ready. The truth is I was scared of losing my paycheck, and I never told her that part.
Five hundred and twenty. That's how many evenings I gave my store idea over five years, and I worked it out on the back of a pay stub in a parked car.
There's a printed refund policy in my work locker with one line circled in pen and a question written in the margin.
